bull_thesis: The bull case is that a genuinely excellent, newly profitable rare-disease franchise has been repriced as though its growth were over, when in fact only the shape of the growth changed. Start with what is verified. Alnylam crossed $1 billion of product revenue in a single quarter for the first time in the first quarter of 2026, and Amvuttra alone crossed $1 billion in the second quarter, with total product revenue up about 74% year over year to roughly $1.2 billion. The company has now printed four consecutive profitable quarters (net income of $251M, $186M, $206M and $164M from the third quarter of 2025 through the second quarter of 2026), against a full-year loss of $2.18 per share as recently as fiscal 2024. Trailing-twelve-month diluted earnings are $5.92 per share and trailing free cash flow is $543 million. This is no longer a story stock; it is a profitable specialty pharmaceutical business that happens to still be growing at a high double-digit rate. Second, the competitive picture improved, not deteriorated. On 9 July 2026 AstraZeneca and Ionis reported that eplontersen (Wainua) missed its primary endpoint in the CARDIO-TTRansform Phase 3 trial in the heart form of TTR amyloidosis. The nearest gene-silencing competitor effectively removed itself from the cardiomyopathy race. Notably that trial showed no treatment effect in patients already taking a stabilizer, which independently validates Alnylam's positioning of Amvuttra as a first-line, stand-alone therapy rather than an add-on. Third, the addressable market is barely touched. Management has said consistently across all five calls in this file that roughly 80% of the global addressable population remains untreated and, as of the first quarter of 2026, that an estimated 200,000 patients with the heart form remain undiagnosed. Access is not the constraint: over 90% of patients have first-line coverage with no step therapy required, most with zero out-of-pocket cost, and adherence runs above 90%. Fourth, the platform is real and broad. Six invented medicines are on the market, more than 25 programmes are in clinical development, and partnered assets throw off royalties from Novartis, Regeneron and Sanofi — roughly $360 million a year of high-margin collaboration revenue that most investors implicitly value at zero. Nucresiran, the next-generation TTR drug in Phase 3, carries no royalty obligation, which is why management believes operating margins could reach the mid-40s after 2030. The conditions this case requires: that the first-line, diagnosis-driven growth curve picks up the slack as the one-time pool of stabilizer-progressing patients finishes converting; that the roughly 25% annual growth ambition through 2030 survives in some recognisable form; that net price erosion stays in the mid-single digits rather than accelerating; and that nucresiran reads out well enough to extend the franchise past Amvuttra's exclusivity. If those hold, the parts are worth far more than today's price.
bear_thesis: The bear case is not that Alnylam is a bad business — it is that the market was paying for a growth algorithm the company itself has now withdrawn, and the remaining price still embeds most of it. On 30 July 2026 Alnylam cut 2026 total product revenue guidance to $4.7-5.1 billion from $4.9-5.3 billion and missed on adjusted earnings ($1.84 against $2.05 expected). The stock fell 28% in a day on a roughly 4% guidance reduction, which tells you the market was not repricing this year — it was repricing the terminal size of the franchise. The stated cause is damning in its simplicity: second-line demand, which the company had presented as durable, was a one-time backlog of patients progressing on stabilizer therapy who had been waiting for a new option. Read the first-quarter 2026 call again and management described that exact mechanism itself — a new prescriber's second-line scripts 'reduced to a normalized level' once their existing stabilizer base is transitioned — and in the same call reaffirmed guidance and promised 'more substantial quarter-over-quarter growth over the balance of the year.' Ninety-one days later it cut. Either the company did not connect its own framework to its own forecast, or it did. Multiple plaintiffs' firms opened securities-fraud investigations on 30-31 July 2026 pointed at precisely that gap. The arithmetic inside the new guidance is the real bear point: first-half 2026 product revenue was roughly $2.24 billion, so the guide implies second-half revenue of $2.46-2.86 billion, meaning quarterly revenue at the low end runs roughly flat against the second quarter. The sequential curve is flattening. Second, the margin story is deteriorating quietly. Gross margin has gone from 84.2% in the third quarter of 2025 to 81.9% in the first quarter of 2026 to 76.9% in the second quarter — seven points in three quarters, steeper than the 'mid-single-digit' annual net-price decline management guides to. Germany's price was already reset lower; most-favoured-nation international pricing and the Inflation Reduction Act's Part D redesign are still to come; and generic tafamidis, following Pfizer's settlement, will hand payers a cheap oral comparator to anchor against. Third, the balance sheet is weaker than the headline. Interest expense was $82 million in the second quarter against $1.27 billion of stated debt — an implied rate no lender charges — which together with $1.47 billion of 'other non-current liabilities' is the signature of a royalty-monetisation financing: a slice of future product royalties sold for cash up front, accreting non-cash interest. The headline $2.04 billion of net cash overstates the true cushion, which is closer to $0.5-1.0 billion. Fourth, concentration. TTR is roughly 85% of product revenue; this is one drug in one disease. And the company's own best margin outcome requires nucresiran cannibalising Amvuttra. Fifth, insiders. Zero open-market purchases against 73 open-market sales (23,132 shares), with the stock 58% below its 52-week high of $495.55 and 3% off its low. Not one insider has stepped in. What confirms the bear: a third-quarter print in late October 2026 that lands at the low end of the revised guide, or any further trim; gross margin below 76%; or a soft full CARDIO-TTRansform dataset at the European Society of Cardiology congress in late August 2026 that reads across badly to combination use.
consensus_delta: Framed for a value candidate, the question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a business with stable or growing earnings power. Our answer is no — and that is where we part company with the bulls rather than with the street. The five freshest analyst price targets, all dated 31 July 2026 and therefore struck after the crash, average about $348 (Martin Auster $420, Luca Issi $350, Oppenheimer $350, Paul Matteis $318, Morgan Stanley $300). Those targets are roughly 70% above the current price and, in our reading, still capitalise the withdrawn growth algorithm. The specific street assumption we believe is wrong is the durability of the 'over 25% revenue CAGR through 2030' ambition management set out in February 2026 and reaffirmed for 2027 on that same call. The company has not repeated it since 30 July. The arithmetic inside the revised guidance is the tell: with first-half product revenue of about $2.24 billion and a full-year guide of $4.7-5.1 billion, the implied second half is $2.46-2.86 billion, meaning quarterly revenue at the low end runs roughly flat against the second quarter's approximately $1.2 billion. A franchise whose sequential revenue is flattening one year into its main launch is not compounding at 25% a year through 2030, and price targets that assume it is will keep drifting down — the analyst-target velocity is already negative 12% against the year-ago average, and the trailing-year cohort of 37 targets averaged $450 against $389 in the last month. The second, subtler disagreement is with the bear side of the street, which now treats the guidance cut as evidence of franchise impairment. It is not. A roughly 4% revenue reduction, caused by the exhaustion of a one-time backlog of patients switching off stabilizer therapy, in a disease where management estimates 200,000 patients remain undiagnosed and where the nearest gene-silencing competitor failed its Phase 3 cardiomyopathy trial on 9 July 2026, is a change in the growth path, not the destruction of it. Both sides are wrong in opposite directions, which is exactly why the honest answer lands on top of the market price. Where we do have a real edge is on the balance sheet: the street and the screener both carry roughly $2.04 billion of net cash as a clean add-back. The $82 million of quarterly interest expense against $1.27 billion of stated debt, plus $1.47 billion of other non-current liabilities, says a meaningful slice of future royalties has already been sold forward. That is worth several dollars a share of overstatement in most published models.
forcing_function: For a value candidate the question is what event forces the market to re-rate, and the honest answer for Alnylam is that no such event is currently scheduled. The three dated items in the field are tests, not triggers. The third-quarter 2026 earnings report in late October is the first check on the revised guidance and can plausibly move the stock in either direction, but a company confirming its own reduced guidance is not a re-rating event — it is the absence of a further disappointment. The full CARDIO-TTRansform dataset at the European Society of Cardiology congress in late August 2026 is a third-party readout that can only hurt or be neutral for Alnylam's combination positioning; its favourable half already fired on 9 July 2026 when the topline miss removed the nearest competitor. Nucresiran, the genuine franchise-extending asset, is not expected to be approved until 2028 for the nerve form and 2030 for the heart form — far outside any reasonable holding-period horizon for a re-rating thesis. What would actually force the market's hand, and none of it is dated: two or three consecutive quarters of first-line-driven sequential growth that demonstrably replaces the exhausted second-line pool, which would restore the multi-year growth algorithm; a formal re-affirmation or credible re-basing of the 2030 targets with the arithmetic shown; the first meaningful insider open-market purchase, which would signal that the people with the best information believe the price is wrong; or a large-cap pharmaceutical acquirer moving on a de-risked $5 billion-revenue rare-disease franchise now available at half its prior price, in what the regime read describes as a record merger-and-acquisition year with pharmaceutical and biotech volume already exceeding all of 2025. That last possibility is real but entirely speculative and cannot be underwritten. In short: the catalyst that mattered has fired, and the next one that matters is two years away.
valley_of_death: There is no financing cliff here — this is a profitable company with roughly $3.3 billion of cash and short-term investments and $543 million of trailing free cash flow. The risk in the next three to nine months is entirely to the narrative and the multiple, not to solvency. Four specific hazards. First, the third-quarter print in late October 2026 is the first test of the revised guidance, and the low end of that guidance implies roughly flat sequential revenue; a print at or below the low end, or any further trim, converts 'one-time normalisation' into 'the growth rate is structurally lower' and there is no valuation support beneath the shares if that happens. Second, the full CARDIO-TTRansform dataset is due at the European Society of Cardiology congress in late August 2026. The topline already showed no treatment effect for eplontersen in patients on a background stabilizer. If the detailed data hardens that finding into a class-level conclusion, the combination and add-on use that supported Amvuttra's second-line volumes gets a scientific headwind on top of the commercial one. Third, margin. Gross margin has fallen from 84.2% in the third quarter of 2025 to 76.9% in the second quarter of 2026. Research and development is running at roughly 32% of revenue and management has committed to about 30% through 2030. If price erosion runs ahead of the guided mid-single digits — with most-favoured-nation international pricing, the Inflation Reduction Act's Part D redesign, the German reset already taken and generic tafamidis arriving — earnings can disappoint even on in-line revenue. Fourth, the securities-fraud investigations opened on 30-31 July 2026. These follow essentially every large one-day drop and are not evidence of wrongdoing, but they impose legal cost, a discovery overhang, and a reason for quality-oriented institutional buyers to wait. On the market backdrop: the current regime read is explicit that rate-cut theses are dead, that positioning is full with fund-manager cash at a formal sell signal, and that negative surprises travel farther than positive ones. A company that just cut guidance is exactly the kind of name that gets punished twice in that tape.
positioning_washout: The shareholder base here is growth and biotech-specialist money, not yield-focused or income holders, so there is no dividend cut to force mechanical liquidation. What there is instead is a slower, more corrosive kind of selling. Alnylam ran from a loss-making platform story to a $60 billion-plus company on the strength of a launch narrative; the holders who bought that narrative are momentum and growth-mandate buyers, and a 28% single-day drop on a guidance cut is precisely the trigger that ends a growth mandate's tolerance. The technical evidence says that redistribution is underway but not finished: the shares sit 58% below the 52-week high of $495.55, about 41% below the 200-day average of $349 and 29% below the 50-day average of $288, and only 3% above the 52-week low of $197.81. A stock this far below both moving averages is one where every rally meets holders who are still underwater. The smart-money score of 28 out of 100 and neutral institutional flow of 50 out of 100 confirm no accumulation is yet visible. Most telling is the insider record: zero open-market purchases against 73 open-market sales totalling 23,132 shares. In a genuine capitulation on a franchise management believes in, insiders buy. None have. That absence is the single cleanest argument that the wash-out is not complete and that the marginal buyer has not yet appeared. On the other side, the free float is large and liquid (about 4.5 million shares traded on the last session), there is no index-deletion risk at a $27.5 billion market capitalisation, and there is no leverage in the capital structure that could force a distressed sale. So this is an orderly, grinding change of ownership from growth hands to value hands rather than a violent forced unwind — and the point at which value hands are decisively paid to step in is lower than today's price.
moderator_conclusion: Pass for now — and this is a continuation of the same view we took on 2 August 2026, not a new one. Nothing dated has emerged since that record, so the verdict and conviction are carried forward unchanged; what follows is a fuller parts-based valuation of the same facts. The finding is uncomfortable because Alnylam is a genuinely good company. It has done what very few biotechnology firms ever do: invented a drug class, commercialised six medicines, and crossed into sustained profitability, with four consecutive profitable quarters and trailing-twelve-month earnings of $5.92 a share. Its nearest gene-silencing competitor failed its Phase 3 heart trial on 9 July 2026. Roughly 80% of the addressable patient population remains untreated. None of that is in dispute. The problem is price against parts. Valuing the business by its pieces — the TTR franchise at a bit over four times next year's revenue, the rare-disease franchise, the royalty and collaboration stream, a risk-adjusted credit for the non-TTR pipeline, and a deliberately conservative balance-sheet add-back — gets to roughly $210 a share against a market price of $205.52. There is no margin of safety, which is the only thing this book is built to buy. Two judgements drive that. The first is the balance sheet: the headline $2.04 billion of net cash is not what it looks like. Interest expense of $82 million a quarter against $1.27 billion of stated debt, sitting beside $1.47 billion of other non-current liabilities, is the fingerprint of a royalty-monetisation financing — a slice of future product economics already sold. We credit roughly $0.6 billion, not $2.04 billion. The second is the growth multiple. On 30 July 2026 the company cut its 2026 product revenue guidance to $4.7-5.1 billion and explained the cut by saying second-line demand had normalised after an early period inflated by pent-up patients switching off stabilizer therapy. Read the first-quarter call from three months earlier and management described that exact mechanism itself, then reaffirmed guidance and promised stronger sequential growth in the same breath. That is not fraud, but it is a demonstrated failure to read its own demand curve, and it is why we will not underwrite the 'over 25% growth a year through 2030' ambition at face value. The arithmetic inside the new guidance implies second-half quarterly revenue running roughly flat against the second quarter at the low end. On the market backdrop: the current regime read holds the hard-binary biotechnology lane as the thinnest edge available for a third consecutive run, treats the tape as efficiently priced there, and warns that in full positioning negative surprises travel farther than positive ones. Applying that tilt does not change the answer here so much as confirm it — but it is worth being explicit that we are not down-rating this name because its catalyst is spent. A fired catalyst on a clean franchise is neither a plus nor a penalty in this book, and if the residual value case offered a real discount we would take it. It does not. The moat is narrow and holding rather than widening: real intellectual property around RNA interference and the delivery chemistry, real regulatory exclusivity, real switching friction in a chronic severe disease — but roughly 85% of product revenue in one drug, gross margin down seven points in three quarters, guided perpetual mid-single-digit price erosion, and economics encumbered by royalties the next-generation product will not carry. Finally, the sentiment evidence. With the shares 58% below their high and 3% off their low, not one insider has bought on the open market, against 73 sales. When the people who know the launch curve best decline to buy the wash-out, an outside committee should not front-run them. The level that would change this: the adverse parts case is about $120 a share, and a price in the $150s would put a real discount to base-case fair value on the table for a profitable franchise with a broken narrative — that is the setup this book exists to buy. # Alnylam Pharmaceuticals (ALNY) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Forensic dossier prepared 2026-08-03. Sources: five consecutive quarterly earnings-call transcripts (Q1 2025 through Q1 2026) supplied in the transcript bundle; the screener's financial block; and — because the bundle stops before it — the 30 July 2026 second-quarter release and the market reaction to it, verified through Financial Modeling Prep's filings, quote and news feeds. Price used throughout: $205.52 per share (Nasdaq, US dollars), the last close as of this writing.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these five calls Alnylam told one story, and told it very well, right up until the moment the story broke.

**The opening (Q1 2025).** The frame was "three core elements": leadership in TTR amyloidosis — a rare, fatal disease in which a mis-folded protein called transthyretin, or TTR, builds up in nerves and heart muscle — plus growth through innovation, plus financial discipline. Amvuttra had just been approved for the heart form of the disease (ATTR cardiomyopathy, or ATTR-CM) in the final days of the quarter. Revenue was $469 million in combined product sales, up 28%. Management was careful: "it's still early days."

**The acceleration (Q2 2025 through Q4 2025).** The caution evaporated, and for good reason. Alnylam raised its own full-year revenue guidance twice inside six months — from a $2.05–2.25 billion range to $2.65–2.80 billion in July 2025, then to $2.95–3.05 billion in October 2025. Chief Executive Yvonne Greenstreet's language moved from "encouraged" to "firing on all cylinders" (Q2 2025). By the February 2026 call the company declared GAAP profitability for full-year 2025 and unveiled "Alnylam 2030" — a five-year plan built on a headline claim of "over 25% revenue CAGR through 2030" (compound annual growth rate, the average yearly growth rate) and a 30% non-GAAP operating margin across the period, with a hint that margins could reach "the mid-40s post 2030" once nucresiran, its next-generation TTR drug, arrives without royalty obligations.

**The first strain (Q1 2026, 30 April).** Revenue passed $1 billion in a quarter for the first time. But the composition of that growth changed tone. Commercial chief Tolga Tanguler introduced a new and, in hindsight, load-bearing explanation of the launch mechanics: a new prescriber's early use is "relatively balanced between first and second lines," where second-line use comes from "moving that prescriber's existing base of patients progressing on stabilizer onto Amvuttra… Over time, as the existing base of stabilizer patients is transitioned, we generally see that prescriber's new second-line scripts reduced to a normalized level." That sentence describes a one-time backlog being worked off. Management presented it as a healthy maturation. It was in fact the arithmetic of the guidance cut three months later. In the same call the company said it "remain[ed] confident in our 2026 TTR revenue guidance" and expected "more substantial quarter-over-quarter growth… over the balance of the year."

**The break (Q2 2026, 30 July — outside the transcript bundle, verified from the filing and news).** Amvuttra topped $1 billion in a single quarter for the first time and total product revenue rose about 74% year over year to roughly $1.2 billion. And the stock fell 28% in a day. Alnylam cut 2026 total product-revenue guidance to $4.7–5.1 billion from $4.9–5.3 billion — a roughly $200 million reduction concentrated in the TTR franchise — and attributed it to second-line demand "normalizing" after an early launch period inflated by pent-up demand from stabilizer patients. Adjusted earnings of $1.84 per share missed the $2.05 consensus. Within 24 hours at least four plaintiffs' law firms announced securities-fraud investigations.

**What was quietly dropped.** The "P5x25" goal set is retired and celebrated. What has not been re-affirmed since 30 July is the "over 25% revenue CAGR through 2030" claim that anchors the entire 2030 plan — and that claim, not the $200 million, is what the market repriced.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim (quarter) | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Firing on all cylinders" (Q2 2025) | Revenue $773.7M, but operating income −$16.2M and net loss −$66.3M | **Poorer than the story.** In mid-2025 the company was still losing money at the operating line while describing itself in maximal terms. |
| Sustainable GAAP profitability from 2025 (Q4 2025) | Delivered. Q3 2025 net income $251.1M, Q4 $186.4M, Q1 2026 $206.0M, Q2 2026 $164.5M — four straight profitable quarters; trailing-twelve-month diluted EPS $5.92 | **Matches.** This one is real and is the single most important fact in the file. |
| "Over 25% revenue CAGR through 2030" (Q4 2025) | 2026 product guidance now $4.7–5.1B against roughly $3.0B in 2025. First half 2026 product revenue was ~$2.24B, so the guide implies second-half revenue of $2.46–2.86B — at the low end, roughly flat against the second quarter's run-rate | **Under pressure.** Full-year 2026 growth is still large, but the *sequential* curve flattens inside the guidance. That is what a decelerating franchise looks like from the inside. |
| Access is "just not a barrier"; step edits "incredibly minimal" (Q2 2025, Q1 2026) | Corroborated by the revenue curve: US TTR revenue went $383M (Q2 2025) → $543M (Q3) → ~$652M (Q4) → ~$711M (Q1 2026) | **Matches.** Payer access genuinely was not the bottleneck. |
| Net price to decline "mid-single-digit" per year (Q3 2025, Q4 2025) | Gross margin has slipped from 84.2% in Q3 2025 to 81.9% in Q1 2026 to 76.9% in Q2 2026 | **Matches, and it is getting worse than "gradual."** A seven-point gross-margin give-back in three quarters is more than price alone usually explains; it deserves a direct question. |

**The caveat the headline net-cash figure hides.** Interest expense was $82.1 million in the second quarter alone — roughly $328 million annualized against $1.27 billion of stated debt. No lender charges 26%. That gap, together with $1.47 billion sitting in "other non-current liabilities," is the signature of a royalty-monetisation financing: Alnylam sold a slice of its own future product royalties for cash up front, and the non-cash accretion on that obligation runs through interest expense. It is a genuine claim on future Amvuttra economics. Treating the full $2.04 billion as free money in a sum-of-the-parts calculation (valuing each business line separately, then adding the balance sheet) overstates the cushion materially. The honest cushion is closer to $0.5–1.0 billion.

**Returns.** The screener's ROIC of −10.3% (return on invested capital) is a stale fiscal-year artifact from the loss years; on a trailing-twelve-month basis the company now earns roughly $1.0 billion of operating income. Returns are inflecting sharply upward. Nothing in this file supports an "eroding returns" read on the current trajectory — the pressure is on the growth rate and the price per dose, not on profitability.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising through Q4 2025, then abruptly defensive.**

- **Q1 2025 — measured.** "It's still early days, and there is more work to do." Specific, hedged, credible.
- **Q2 2025 — maximal.** "Firing on all cylinders." "A remarkable achievement." Guidance raised $575 million at the midpoint. This is the peak-confidence quarter.
- **Q3 2025 — confident but with the first technical hedges.** Gross-to-net deductions (the discounts and rebates subtracted from list price) enter the vocabulary as a reason reported growth trails demand growth. Management also announced it would stop reporting the health-system setup metric because it was "effectively complete" — the first launch disclosure to be retired.
- **Q4 2025 — strategic and long-dated.** The story moves from this quarter's numbers to a five-year plan. Long-horizon goals are the natural refuge when near-term acceleration is about to slow.
- **Q1 2026 — the pivot.** The prepared remarks introduce a framework for why second-line prescribing declines per prescriber over time, while simultaneously promising "more substantial quarter-over-quarter growth… over the balance of the year." Those two statements sit uneasily together. Management was explaining the deceleration mechanism and denying the deceleration in the same call.
- **Q2 2026 — capitulation on the number.** Guidance cut, the cause named as normalization of a demand pool the company had previously described as durable.

Note also a specificity ratchet that runs the wrong way: in Q2 2025 management gave a hard patient count (approximately 1,400 cardiomyopathy patients on therapy). By Q1 2026 the disclosed metrics had become softer — prescriber counts and share-of-first-line percentages rather than absolute patients on drug. Disclosure got less falsifiable as the growth got harder.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium.** This is a company with an excellent delivery record and one serious, recent, self-inflicted wound.

The record: 2025 guidance was raised twice and beaten. The initial $2.05–2.25 billion became $2.65–2.80 billion in July, then $2.95–3.05 billion in October, and the year closed above $3 billion. That is over-delivery, repeated. The screener's beat rate of five of the last seven quarters (71%) is consistent.

The wound: on 30 April 2026 management explicitly reaffirmed 2026 TTR guidance and forecast "more substantial quarter-over-quarter growth… over the balance of the year." Ninety-one days later it cut that guidance and explained the cut with a demand dynamic it had *itself described in detail on that same April call*. Either the company did not connect its own prescriber-behaviour framework to its own forecast, or it did and reaffirmed anyway. Neither reading is flattering, and the plaintiffs' firms circling since 30 July are pointed at exactly this gap.

There is no sandbagging pattern here. The 2025 raises were genuine upside surprises, which makes the 2026 miss more informative, not less: this management team guides to what it believes, and in April 2026 it believed something wrong about its own launch curve.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three themes recur, and the analysts were closer to right than management on all three.

**First-line versus second-line mix — asked every single quarter, never answered numerically.** Gena Wang of Barclays asked directly in Q2 2025 whether more than half of the 1,400 patients were first-line. The answer: "our uptake has been broad and balanced." She asked again in Q3 2025 — "roughly 50-50 or second-line slightly higher?" The answer: "we are increasingly getting more competitive in first-line." Four consecutive quarters of a specific numerical question met with a directional adjective. That undisclosed mix is precisely the variable that broke the guidance. This is the most important pattern in the file.

**The stabilizer combination question.** Mike Ulz of Morgan Stanley asked about combination use in Q2 2025; Ritu Baral of TD Cowen and others returned to it repeatedly. Management consistently minimised it — "a very small portion." The combination and switch pool turned out to be the launch's engine, and its exhaustion is the guidance cut.

**Competitive read-through.** In Q4 2025, Evercore's analyst asked what a rival gene-silencing drug's data would mean. Chief R&D Officer Pushkal Garg predicted the competitor trial would succeed: "Our expectation is the study will be positive." On 9 July 2026 the opposite happened — AstraZeneca and Ionis reported that eplontersen (Wainua) missed its primary endpoint in the CARDIO-TTRansform Phase 3 cardiomyopathy trial, and Alnylam's stock rose on the news. Management's competitive forecast was wrong in Alnylam's favour, which is a pleasant kind of wrong but still a miss on a question they were asked to judge.

**What analysts are not yet pressing hard enough:** the gross-margin slide, and what the royalty-monetisation obligation costs shareholders in cash terms as the franchise scales.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The reaffirm-then-cut sequence (30 April → 30 July 2026).** Guidance confirmed, then reduced 91 days later for a reason management had already articulated. The single most damaging item in the file.

🔴 **Four consecutive quarters of refusing a specific first-line/second-line split (Q2 2025 – Q1 2026)** on the exact metric that later broke the forecast.

🔴 **Gross margin from 84.2% (Q3 2025) to 76.9% (Q2 2026)** — steeper than the "mid-single-digit" annual net-price decline management guided to.

🔴 **Securities-fraud investigations announced by multiple plaintiffs' firms on 30–31 July 2026.** These are routine after a large one-day drop and are not evidence of wrongdoing, but they impose real legal cost and a discovery overhang.

🔴 **Insider behaviour: zero open-market purchases against 73 open-market sales (23,132 shares).** With the stock 58% below its 52-week high of $495.55 and 3% off its low, not one insider has bought. That is the cleanest sentiment reading available.

🔴 **Interest expense of $82 million a quarter against $1.27 billion of debt**, signalling a royalty-monetisation obligation that the headline net-cash figure does not capture.

🟢 **The profitability inflection is real and verified.** Four straight profitable quarters; trailing-twelve-month diluted EPS of $5.92 against a full-year loss of $2.18 per share as recently as fiscal 2024.

🟢 **Amvuttra crossed $1 billion in a single quarter (Q2 2026)** — a genuine blockbuster from a company that a decade ago had no approved product.

🟢 **The principal competitive threat to the cardiomyopathy franchise removed itself on 9 July 2026** when eplontersen missed its endpoint. Notably, that trial showed no treatment effect in patients already on a stabilizer — which validates Alnylam's monotherapy positioning and simultaneously helps explain why the combination/second-line pool was never as deep as hoped.

🟢 **Payer access delivered exactly as promised.** Over 90% of patients with first-line access, most with zero out-of-pocket cost, adherence above 90% (Q1 2026). Management said this would happen, and it did.

🟢 **Platform breadth is not a slogan.** Six invented medicines on the market, more than 25 clinical programmes, partnered assets generating royalties from Novartis, Regeneron and Sanofi.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary of maturity arrived before the numbers did.** "Gross-to-net deductions," "normalized level," "channel inventory," "customary insurance reauthorization dynamics" — this is the language of a launch settling into a base business, and it entered the transcripts in Q3 2025, three quarters before the guidance cut. The words led the arithmetic.

**Retiring a disclosure is a signal.** In Q3 2025 management announced it would stop reporting health-system setup "on future calls." The stated reason was completion. The effect was one fewer public yardstick.

**The nucresiran subtext.** In Q4 2025 management noted nucresiran carries "no royalty obligations" and could push operating margins "to the mid-40s post 2030." Read the other way, that says today's Amvuttra economics are royalty-encumbered — a margin ceiling on the current franchise that only a product replacement lifts. The company's own best margin story requires cannibalising its only blockbuster.

**Speaker attribution in the Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 transcripts is visibly garbled** (answers assigned to the wrong executives, analyst names crossed). That is a transcription artifact, not a governance signal, but it means individual attributions from those two calls should be read with care.

**Pricing candour is consistent and unflattering, which is a mark in management's favour.** Chief Financial Officer Jeff Poulton has said the same thing three calls running: mid-single-digit annual net-price decline, year one and year two. They are not hiding this.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE.** Not deteriorating — revenue still grew about 74% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, four consecutive quarters have been profitable, and the balance sheet funds the pipeline without dilution. Not strengthening either — the growth algorithm that justified the valuation has been publicly revised down by the company that wrote it, and the sequential revenue curve flattens inside the company's own second-half guidance.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** This is not a question about whether Alnylam is a good company. It plainly is. The question is what the terminal size of the TTR franchise is, and the honest answer changed on 30 July 2026 — not because of the $200 million, but because the company demonstrated it could not distinguish a one-time backlog of stabilizer patients from a durable run-rate in its own launch. Everything in the valuation past 2028 rests on a first-line diagnosis-driven growth curve that has never been observed at scale, forecast by a team that just mis-read the curve it *had* observed. Size to that uncertainty, not to the 74% headline.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and the width is holding rather than widening.** The moat type is intangible-asset and regulatory: a patent estate around RNA interference and the GalNAc delivery chemistry that gets these drugs into the right tissue, plus orphan and regulatory exclusivity, plus the switching friction of a chronic therapy in a severe disease where physicians do not casually move a stable patient. The evidence supports "real but narrow," not "wide": the franchise is one drug in one disease (TTR is roughly 85% of product revenue); gross margin is falling seven points in three quarters; management guides to perpetual mid-single-digit annual price erosion; and Amvuttra's economics are royalty-encumbered in a way the next-generation product is not. Against that, returns on capital are inflecting strongly upward from a loss base and the nearest competitor's cardiomyopathy trial just failed. Net: narrow and stable.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The structural force is reimbursement compression — most-favoured-nation international pricing, the Inflation Reduction Act's Part D redesign, the German price reset already taken, and the arrival of generic tafamidis creating a cheap oral comparator that payers will anchor to. This does not impair the terminal value of a therapy that demonstrably reduces cardiovascular death; it compresses the price per patient and slows the pace at which a silencer displaces a stabilizer. The base is not structurally shrinking — it is structurally growing more slowly and at a lower price than the 2030 plan assumes.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither, which is the awkward answer. At $205.52 the shares are not obviously cheap on the parts: strip out the balance sheet honestly and the market is paying roughly five times this year's revenue for a franchise whose growth rate the company just cut. A 58% drawdown from the high does not by itself create value when the high embedded a growth rate that has since been withdrawn. This is a fair price for a good business, not a mispricing.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

By the February 2026 call the company declared GAAP profitability for full-year 2025 and unveiled "Alnylam 2030" — a five-year plan built on a headline claim of "over 25% revenue CAGR through 2030" (compound annual growth rate, the average yearly growth rate) and a 30% non-GAAP operating margin across the period, with a hint that margins could reach "the mid-40s post 2030" once nucresiran, its next-generation TTR drug, arrives without royalty obligations.

**The first strain (Q1 2026, 30 April).** Revenue passed $1 billion in a quarter for the first time. But the composition of that growth changed tone. Commercial chief Tolga Tanguler introduced a new and, in hindsight, load-bearing explanation of the launch mechanics: a new prescriber's early use is "relatively balanced between first and second lines," where second-line use comes from "moving that prescriber's existing base of patients progressing on stabilizer onto Amvuttra… Over time, as the existing base of stabilizer patients is transitioned, we generally see that prescriber's new second-line scripts reduced to a normalized level." That sentence describes a one-time backlog being worked off. Management presented it as a healthy maturation. It was in fact the arithmetic of the guidance cut three months later. In the same call the company said it "remain[ed] confident in our 2026 TTR revenue guidance" and expected "more substantial quarter-over-quarter growth… over the balance of the year."

**The break (Q2 2026, 30 July — outside the transcript bundle, verified from the filing and news).** Amvuttra topped $1 billion in a single quarter for the first time and total product revenue rose about 74% year over year to roughly $1.2 billion. And the stock fell 28% in a day. Alnylam cut 2026 total product-revenue guidance to $4.7–5.1 billion from $4.9–5.3 billion — a roughly $200 million reduction concentrated in the TTR franchise — and attributed it to second-line demand "normalizing" after an early launch period inflated by pent-up demand from stabilizer patients. Adjusted earnings of $1.84 per share missed the $2.05 consensus. Within 24 hours at least four plaintiffs' law firms announced securities-fraud investigations.

**What was quietly dropped.** The "P5x25" goal set is retired and celebrated. What has not been re-affirmed since 30 July is the "over 25% revenue CAGR through 2030" claim that anchors the entire 2030 plan — and that claim, not the $200 million, is what the market repriced.

First half 2026 product revenue was ~$2.24B, so the guide implies second-half revenue of $2.46–2.86B — at the low end, roughly flat against the second quarter's run-rate | **Under pressure.** Full-year 2026 growth is still large, but the *sequential* curve flattens inside the guidance. That is what a decelerating franchise looks like from the inside. |
| Access is "just not a barrier"; step edits "incredibly minimal" (Q2 2025, Q1 2026) | Corroborated by the revenue curve: US TTR revenue went $383M (Q2 2025) → $543M (Q3) → ~$652M (Q4) → ~$711M (Q1 2026) | **Matches.** Payer access genuinely was not the bottleneck. |
| Net price to decline "mid-single-digit" per year (Q3 2025, Q4 2025) | Gross margin has slipped from 84.2% in Q3 2025 to 81.9% in Q1 2026 to 76.9% in Q2 2026 | **Matches, and it is getting worse than "gradual."** A seven-point gross-margin give-back in three quarters is more than price alone usually explains; it deserves a direct question. |
| "Our fortunes aren't tied to the genericization of the stabilizer class" (Q1 2026) | Untested — generic tafamidis has not arrived yet | **Unproven.** File it as an open claim, not a verified one. |
| Balance sheet is a fortress | Cash and short-term investments $3.31B against total debt of $1.27B at 30 June 2026, so headline net cash of about $2.04B | **Matches on the surface, with a caveat below.** |

**The caveat the headline net-cash figure hides.** Interest expense was $82.1 million in the second quarter alone — roughly $328 million annualized against $1.27 billion of stated debt. No lender charges 26%. That gap, together with $1.47 billion sitting in "other non-current liabilities," is the signature of a royalty-monetisation financing: Alnylam sold a slice of its own future product royalties for cash up front, and the non-cash accretion on that obligation runs through interest expense. It is a genuine claim on future Amvuttra economics. Treating the full $2.04 billion as free money in a sum-of-the-parts calculation (valuing each business line separately, then adding the balance sheet) overstates the cushion materially. The honest cushion is closer to $0.5–1.0 billion.

**Returns.** The screener's ROIC of −10.3% (return on invested capital) is a stale fiscal-year artifact from the loss years; on a trailing-twelve-month basis the company now earns roughly $1.0 billion of operating income. Returns are inflecting sharply upward. Nothing in this file supports an "eroding returns" read on the current trajectory — the pressure is on the growth rate and the price per dose, not on profitability.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising through Q4 2025, then abruptly defensive.**

- **Q1 2025 — measured.** "It's still early days, and there is more work to do." Specific, hedged, credible.
- **Q2 2025 — maximal.** "Firing on all cylinders." "A remarkable achievement." Guidance raised $575 million at the midpoint. This is the peak-confidence quarter.
- **Q3 2025 — confident but with the first technical hedges.** Gross-to-net deductions (the discounts and rebates subtracted from list price) enter the vocabulary as a reason reported growth trails demand growth. Management also announced it would stop reporting the health-system setup metric because it was "effectively complete" — the first launch disclosure to be retired.
- **Q4 2025 — strategic and long-dated.** The story moves from this quarter's numbers to a five-year plan. Long-horizon goals are the natural refuge when near-term acceleration is about to slow.
- **Q1 2026 — the pivot.** The prepared remarks introduce a framework for why second-line prescribing declines per prescriber over time, while simultaneously promising "more substantial quarter-over-quarter growth… over the balance of the year." Those two statements sit uneasily together. Management was explaining the deceleration mechanism and denying the deceleration in the same call.
- **Q2 2026 — capitulation on the number.** Guidance cut, the cause named as normalization of a demand pool the company had previously described as durable.

Note also a specificity ratchet that runs the wrong way: in Q2 2025 management gave a hard patient count (approximately 1,400 cardiomyopathy patients on therapy). By Q1 2026 the disclosed metrics had become softer — prescriber counts and share-of-first-line percentages rather than absolute patients on drug. Disclosure got less falsifiable as the growth got harder.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium.** This is a company with an excellent delivery record and one serious, recent, self-inflicted wound.

The record: 2025 guidance was raised twice and beaten. The initial $2.05–2.25 billion became $2.65–2.80 billion in July, then $2.95–3.05 billion in October, and the year closed above $3 billion. That is over-delivery, repeated. The screener's beat rate of five of the last seven quarters (71%) is consistent.

The wound: on 30 April 2026 management explicitly reaffirmed 2026 TTR guidance and forecast "more substantial quarter-over-quarter growth… over the balance of the year." Ninety-one days later it cut that guidance and explained the cut with a demand dynamic it had *itself described in detail on that same April call*. Either the company did not connect its own prescriber-behaviour framework to its own forecast, or it did and reaffirmed anyway. Neither reading is flattering, and the plaintiffs' firms circling since 30 July are pointed at exactly this gap.

There is no sandbagging pattern here. The 2025 raises were genuine upside surprises, which makes the 2026 miss more informative, not less: this management team guides to what it believes, and in April 2026 it believed something wrong about its own launch curve.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three themes recur, and the analysts were closer to right than management on all three.

**First-line versus second-line mix — asked every single quarter, never answered numerically.** Gena Wang of Barclays asked directly in Q2 2025 whether more than half of the 1,400 patients were first-line. The answer: "our uptake has been broad and balanced." She asked again in Q3 2025 — "roughly 50-50 or second-line slightly higher?" The answer: "we are increasingly getting more competitive in first-line." Four consecutive quarters of a specific numerical question met with a directional adjective. That undisclosed mix is precisely the variable that broke the guidance. This is the most important pattern in the file.

**The stabilizer combination question.** Mike Ulz of Morgan Stanley asked about combination use in Q2 2025; Ritu Baral of TD Cowen and others returned to it repeatedly. Management consistently minimised it — "a very small portion." The combination and switch pool turned out to be the launch's engine, and its exhaustion is the guidance cut.

**Competitive read-through.** In Q4 2025, Evercore's analyst asked what a rival gene-silencing drug's data would mean. Chief R&D Officer Pushkal Garg predicted the competitor trial would succeed: "Our expectation is the study will be positive." On 9 July 2026 the opposite happened — AstraZeneca and Ionis reported that eplontersen (Wainua) missed its primary endpoint in the CARDIO-TTRansform Phase 3 cardiomyopathy trial, and Alnylam's stock rose on the news. Management's competitive forecast was wrong in Alnylam's favour, which is a pleasant kind of wrong but still a miss on a question they were asked to judge.

**What analysts are not yet pressing hard enough:** the gross-margin slide, and what the royalty-monetisation obligation costs shareholders in cash terms as the franchise scales.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The reaffirm-then-cut sequence (30 April → 30 July 2026).** Guidance confirmed, then reduced 91 days later for a reason management had already articulated. The single most damaging item in the file.

🔴 **Four consecutive quarters of refusing a specific first-line/second-line split (Q2 2025 – Q1 2026)** on the exact metric that later broke the forecast.

🔴 **Gross margin from 84.2% (Q3 2025) to 76.9% (Q2 2026)** — steeper than the "mid-single-digit" annual net-price decline management guided to.

🔴 **Securities-fraud investigations announced by multiple plaintiffs' firms on 30–31 July 2026.** These are routine after a large one-day drop and are not evidence of wrongdoing, but they impose real legal cost and a discovery overhang.

🔴 **Insider behaviour: zero open-market purchases against 73 open-market sales (23,132 shares).** With the stock 58% below its 52-week high of $495.55 and 3% off its low, not one insider has bought. That is the cleanest sentiment reading available.

🔴 **Interest expense of $82 million a quarter against $1.27 billion of debt**, signalling a royalty-monetisation obligation that the headline net-cash figure does not capture.

🟢 **The profitability inflection is real and verified.** Four straight profitable quarters; trailing-twelve-month diluted EPS of $5.92 against a full-year loss of $2.18 per share as recently as fiscal 2024.

🟢 **Amvuttra crossed $1 billion in a single quarter (Q2 2026)** — a genuine blockbuster from a company that a decade ago had no approved product.

🟢 **The principal competitive threat to the cardiomyopathy franchise removed itself on 9 July 2026** when eplontersen missed its endpoint. Notably, that trial showed no treatment effect in patients already on a stabilizer — which validates Alnylam's monotherapy positioning and simultaneously helps explain why the combination/second-line pool was never as deep as hoped.

🟢 **Payer access delivered exactly as promised.** Over 90% of patients with first-line access, most with zero out-of-pocket cost, adherence above 90% (Q1 2026). Management said this would happen, and it did.

🟢 **Platform breadth is not a slogan.** Six invented medicines on the market, more than 25 clinical programmes, partnered assets generating royalties from Novartis, Regeneron and Sanofi.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary of maturity arrived before the numbers did.** "Gross-to-net deductions," "normalized level," "channel inventory," "customary insurance reauthorization dynamics" — this is the language of a launch settling into a base business, and it entered the transcripts in Q3 2025, three quarters before the guidance cut. The words led the arithmetic.

**Retiring a disclosure is a signal.** In Q3 2025 management announced it would stop reporting health-system setup "on future calls." The stated reason was completion. The effect was one fewer public yardstick.

**The nucresiran subtext.** In Q4 2025 management noted nucresiran carries "no royalty obligations" and could push operating margins "to the mid-40s post 2030." Read the other way, that says today's Amvuttra economics are royalty-encumbered — a margin ceiling on the current franchise that only a product replacement lifts. The company's own best margin story requires cannibalising its only blockbuster.

**Speaker attribution in the Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 transcripts is visibly garbled** (answers assigned to the wrong executives, analyst names crossed). That is a transcription artifact, not a governance signal, but it means individual attributions from those two calls should be read with care.

**Pricing candour is consistent and unflattering, which is a mark in management's favour.** Chief Financial Officer Jeff Poulton has said the same thing three calls running: mid-single-digit annual net-price decline, year one and year two. They are not hiding this.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE.** Not deteriorating — revenue still grew about 74% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, four consecutive quarters have been profitable, and the balance sheet funds the pipeline without dilution. Not strengthening either — the growth algorithm that justified the valuation has been publicly revised down by the company that wrote it, and the sequential revenue curve flattens inside the company's own second-half guidance.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** This is not a question about whether Alnylam is a good company. It plainly is. The question is what the terminal size of the TTR franchise is, and the honest answer changed on 30 July 2026 — not because of the $200 million, but because the company demonstrated it could not distinguish a one-time backlog of stabilizer patients from a durable run-rate in its own launch. Everything in the valuation past 2028 rests on a first-line diagnosis-driven growth curve that has never been observed at scale, forecast by a team that just mis-read the curve it *had* observed. Size to that uncertainty, not to the 74% headline.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and the width is holding rather than widening.** The moat type is intangible-asset and regulatory: a patent estate around RNA interference and the GalNAc delivery chemistry that gets these drugs into the right tissue, plus orphan and regulatory exclusivity, plus the switching friction of a chronic therapy in a severe disease where physicians do not casually move a stable patient. The evidence supports "real but narrow," not "wide": the franchise is one drug in one disease (TTR is roughly 85% of product revenue); gross margin is falling seven points in three quarters; management guides to perpetual mid-single-digit annual price erosion; and Amvuttra's economics are royalty-encumbered in a way the next-generation product is not. Against that, returns on capital are inflecting strongly upward from a loss base and the nearest competitor's cardiomyopathy trial just failed. Net: narrow and stable.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The structural force is reimbursement compression — most-favoured-nation international pricing, the Inflation Reduction Act's Part D redesign, the German price reset already taken, and the arrival of generic tafamidis creating a cheap oral comparator that payers will anchor to. This does not impair the terminal value of a therapy that demonstrably reduces cardiovascular death; it compresses the price per patient and slows the pace at which a silencer displaces a stabilizer. The base is not structurally shrinking — it is structurally growing more slowly and at a lower price than the 2030 plan assumes.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither, which is the awkward answer. At $205.52 the shares are not obviously cheap on the parts: strip out the balance sheet honestly and the market is paying roughly five times this year's revenue for a franchise whose growth rate the company just cut. A 58% drawdown from the high does not by itself create value when the high embedded a growth rate that has since been withdrawn. This is a fair price for a good business, not a mispricing.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

bull_thesis: Alnylam is one of a handful of biotechnology companies that has invented a drug class, commercialised it, and then crossed into durable profitability. Six approved medicines, four consecutive profitable quarters, and revenue that nearly doubled year on year to $1.29 billion in the June 2026 quarter. The core asset is AMVUTTRA, a quarterly injection for a heart disease caused by a misfolded protein called transthyretin, and the June quarter was the first time that single franchise passed $1 billion in three months, an annual run-rate above $4 billion just fifteen months after launch. The bull case rests on four supports. First, the market is barely tapped: management estimates roughly 200,000 US patients with about 80% still untreated, and the diagnosed population has been growing at around 40% a year without Alnylam's help. Second, the competitive field just improved rather than worsened: on 30 July 2026 the company confirmed that the incumbent oral drug tafamidis is now expected to keep US exclusivity until mid-2031, removing a generic threat investors had pencilled in far earlier, and a rival injectable, eplontersen, failed its large heart-outcomes trial, most likely removing a branded competitor before it arrived. Third, the mix of demand is improving even as the total slows: about 80% of new patient starts are now first-line, meaning patients starting treatment for the first time rather than switching off an older drug, which is the larger and more durable half of the market, and among physicians who have already prescribed AMVUTTRA it accounts for more than half of their new starts. Fourth, only about a third of the prescriber pool has ever written the drug, so the growth plan is arithmetic rather than speculative: reach the other two-thirds. Behind the marketed products sit more than 25 clinical programmes, of which nucresiran matters most, a next-generation silencer with over 95% protein knockdown on twice-yearly dosing, carrying no royalty obligation, targeted at a 2028 launch in nerve disease and 2030 in heart disease. For the bull case to work, three conditions must hold: first-line demand must keep compounding fast enough to more than replace the switch business that has now normalised; net price must keep falling only at the guided mid-single-digit annual rate; and free cash flow must reconverge with reported earnings, because at present it has not.
bear_thesis: The bear case is not that Alnylam is a bad company. It is that the share price still asks to be paid for a growth path management demonstrated on 30 July 2026 it cannot forecast. On that date the company cut its 2026 product revenue guidance to $4.7-5.1 billion, with the whole $200 million reduction falling on the core franchise, and the shares fell 28% the next session. The reason given is the most damaging one available: a large slice of the 2025 demand that set the original forecast was a one-time backlog of patients already failing on the older drug class, who have now been switched and cannot be switched again. That is a permanent reduction in the run-rate, not a timing slip, and it was a fact only Alnylam could see in its own data. The chief financial officer's admission, that they did not get the original guidance right and that they own it, is admirable and also disqualifying for anyone underwriting the 2030 ambition of 25% annual growth, which was reaffirmed on the same call and rests on the same forecasting apparatus. Underneath the profit-and-loss statement sits a harder problem. Free cash flow was $543 million over the trailing twelve months against $808 million of reported net income, and in the first half of 2026 it was only $89 million against $370 million of net income. In the June quarter alone, $223 million of non-cash credits had to be stripped out of net income to reach operating cash flow. Meanwhile the product gross margin fell four points year on year to 75% because the royalty owed to Sanofi rises with volume, net price is guided down mid-single digits every year, Germany has already reset its price, and European reimbursement is being negotiated against a soon-to-be-generic incumbent. The balance sheet is presented as $2.04 billion of net cash, but shareholders' equity is only $1.35 billion, there is $1.47 billion of other long-term liabilities, and cash interest actually paid over three disclosed quarters was roughly $201 million against $1.27 billion of stated debt, a cost of money that does not belong to an ordinary loan book. Add the concentration risk that roughly 89% of product revenue comes from one franchise, a replacement drug that will not launch in the heart indication until 2030 with its pivotal trial newly clouded by a competitor's failure, insider activity that is 73 open-market sales against zero purchases, and a Wall Street price-target average that has fallen from $432.56 over the past year to $295.00 over the past month, with Jefferies publishing $230 on 28 August below the then-current price. What would confirm the bear case: another quarter in which reported profit runs far ahead of free cash flow, or a third-quarter print in late October that does not repeat the June quarter's growth, which management conceded is required in both remaining quarters simply to reach the revised midpoint.
consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is not about the quality of the franchise, which we think is genuinely good, but about two things the market is currently choosing not to price. The first is cash. The market is capitalising $808 million of reported profit at 45 times; we think the number that matters is $543 million of trailing free cash flow, and more pointedly the $89 million generated in the first half of 2026 against $370 million of reported net income over the same two quarters. In the June quarter alone, $223 million of non-cash credits had to be removed from net income to reach operating cash flow. Nobody asked management about this on any of the eight calls we reviewed. The second is what the July guidance cut actually revealed. The consensus reading, echoed in the 16 August Motley Fool piece arguing the sell-off looks overdone, is that the reset was a one-time recalibration on a business still compounding. Our reading is that it demonstrated management could not size the composition of its own demand, specifically how much of the 2025 second-line surge was a backlog that could not repeat, and that this is the single variable on which the whole 25%-a-year path to 2030 depends. A team that misjudged six months of its own proprietary data is not a team whose five-year forecast should be capitalised at a premium multiple. Where we agree with the market: the competitive landscape genuinely improved on 30 July, and we have credited it in the base case.
forcing_function: There is no event on the calendar that forces a re-rating within our horizon, and that is part of why this is a pass rather than a wait-for-the-wash-out. The nearest consequential date is the third-quarter 2026 earnings report around 30 October, which is a test rather than a catalyst: it can confirm the reset or break the story, but the good outcome is merely that management was right, which is already in the price. moderator_conclusion: Pass for now, and this is a continuation of the same view we took on 31 August 2026 and on 2 August before that, not a fresh one. Nothing dated has emerged in the past week that changes the verdict, so it is carried forward; what has changed is the price, and it has changed against us. Alnylam is a genuinely good company and we want to say so clearly before explaining why we are not buying it. It has done what very few biotechnology firms ever do: invented a drug class, commercialised six medicines, and crossed into sustained profitability, with four consecutive profitable quarters and trailing earnings of $5.92 a share. Its main product passed $1 billion in a single quarter fifteen months after launch, in a market that is roughly 80% untreated and where the diagnosed population is growing about 40% a year. On 30 July the competitive landscape improved twice over: the incumbent oral drug will hold US exclusivity to mid-2031, and a rival injectable failed its outcomes trial. We are passing on price. Judged on the value case alone, setting the catalyst and the market backdrop entirely aside, the answer is the same and for the same reason: a fine business at 45 times earnings and 66 times free cash flow, trading above our estimate of its worth, is not a value proposition.
